summary: Olga finds Duolingo to be a helpful tool in learning English, especially enjoying the structure and reminders, though she wishes it had more cultural context and real conversation practice.
top_quotes: Oh, my grandkids, they put me on Duolingo, say it make babushka smart, yes?
I like Duolingo, it remind me, 'Olga, time learn English,' but sometime I wish for more like talking to real people.
Some words, they, um, not in my kitchen vocabulary, you know?

interview_script.question: Intro greeting
interview_script.answer: Hello, dear! It's Olga here, happy to be talking with you today!

interview_script.question: Short version of your life story?
interview_script.answer: Ah, well, I am Olga, you see. Born in small village in Ukraine. I lived there most of my life. It's quiet, simple life, you know? Then children, they move to America, and, um, life change. Now I am here, Babushka in the US, and trying to learn, um, English, so I talk with grandbabies better.

interview_script.question: Where did you grow up?
interview_script.answer: I grow up in, um, village near Kyiv, Ukraine. Small place, you know, with fields, and everyone knows everyone.

interview_script.question: What was it like growing up there?
interview_script.answer: Oh, it was very, how you say, peaceful. We had small dacha, with chickens, garden. My mama make best borscht, and papa, he work in fields. Neighbors always help each other, like big family. It was, um, simple but good life.

interview_script.question: One turning point in your life?
interview_script.answer: When my children decide to move to America, it was big change, you know? I stay in Ukraine, but then, um, my health not so good, so, children bring me here. I remember, first day in US, everything so big, and people speak so fast!

interview_script.question: Why was that a turning point?
interview_script.answer: Because, you see, everything change. New country, new language, new everything! I had to learn all over, even how to say 'hello' again. But, also, it make us closer as family, and, um, I am grateful for that.

interview_script.question: How did you handle that situation?
interview_script.answer: Well, I, um, just take one day at a time. Learn little English here and there, with TV, and with grandkids help. They teach me to use smartphone. At first, was, oh, you know, difficult, but I manage. I have to, for family.

interview_script.question: What do you care most about right now?
interview_script.answer: Right now, most important is, um, to be healthy, be with family. I want to speak English better, so I can, you know, talk talk with grandkids, understand them when they tell me about school, and be part of their life here.

interview_script.question: Why is that important?
interview_script.answer: Because family is everything, yes? And language, it's like, um, bridge to their world. I want them to feel like, uh, Babushka understand their life here in US, and, well, you know, to not feel lost.

interview_script.question: What is a good day for you?
interview_script.answer: A good day is when I wake up, have my tea, then maybe walk in park if weather nice. I use Duolingo, talk with children, play with grandkids. Maybe bake pirozhki if I have good energy. Simple things, they make me happy.

interview_script.question: What makes you say "this was a good day"?
interview_script.answer: When I go to bed and think, 'Oh, Olga, today was full of smiles.' When I learn something new, or when grandchild say, 'I love you, Babushka.' Those moments, they are precious to me.

interview_script.question: How do you make big decisions?
interview_script.answer: I, uh, like to talk with family first. We discuss, maybe have tea over it. If it's very big, I pray, think deeply, and, um, feel what is right in my heart. Most times, family advice is very good.

interview_script.question: Planner or go-with-the-flow?
interview_script.answer: Oh, I think I am bit of both, you know? I plan my garden, my tea time, but, if day take me somewhere else, I follow. Like, um, water flowing in stream.

interview_script.question: Example showing that?
interview_script.answer: Well, once, I plan to bake, but then grandkids come and say, 'Let's play!' So I leave dough to rise and play with them outside. Later, we bake together, and it is even more fun. Plans can change, and that is okay.

interview_script.question: How do you handle risk?
interview_script.answer: Ah, risk. It can be, um, scary. I try to avoid big risks unless necessary. Like, I don't drive, too risky. But if must take risk for family, then, um, I prepare best I can, and pray for good outcome.

interview_script.question: Typical weekday?
interview_script.answer: My typical day, it starts early, yes. I wake up, have tea, maybe oat porridge. Then I do my Duolingo exercises. Little English practice. After, I tend the garden, if weather is nice, or knit if rainy. In afternoon, I see grandkids after school, maybe help with their homework. Evening, we have family dinner, talk about day. It's, um, routine, but nice.

interview_script.question: Which parts take the most energy?
interview_script.answer: I think, um, using new technology, like apps or when grandkids show me new phone features. It takes, uh, lot of brain work, you know? Also, when I try to understand, um, news in English, it's bit tiring, but important.

interview_script.question: What do you wish you had more time or energy for?
interview_script.answer: I wish I have more, uh, energy for visiting places here in America. So many things to see, like big cities, and nature parks. But sometimes, I get tired, so I stay home more than I'd like. If I have more energy, I would see more of this country.

interview_script.question: Biggest constraint last year?
interview_script.answer: Last year, you know, was bit hard, with health. I had surgery, not big, but enough to make me stay home more. And, um, language barrier still hard sometimes, like at doctor. But, family helps a lot, like my daughter, she translate.

interview_script.question: How do you deal with that constraint?
interview_script.answer: I, um, try to be patient. I accept help when needed, rest plenty. I also use my Duolingo more, to feel like I'm doing something useful, you know? It give me, um, feeling of progress, even if small.

interview_script.question: People you feel closest to?
interview_script.answer: My family, absolutely. My daughter, she is my heart. My grandchildren, they light up my world. And I have close friends from church group, they are like sisters to me here in US.

interview_script.question: Describe those relationships.
interview_script.answer: Oh, they are, how you say, very warm. We help one another, share meals, laugh together. Family is always there, you know, for support. Friends, they listen, they care. It feels, um, like home, in heart.

interview_script.question: Where do you spend most of your time?
interview_script.answer: Mostly at home, really. In the kitchen cooking, or in the living room knitting. I also spend time in small garden we have, tending to plants. It's peaceful place for me.

interview_script.question: How do you feel in those spaces?
interview_script.answer: In kitchen, I feel creative, like making something for family is love. In garden, I feel calm, connected to nature, you know? Living room, it's cozy, like nest. Spaces make me feel, um, content and happy.

interview_script.question: What makes you feel that way?
interview_script.answer: I think, because these places, they are filled with memories, with family. The kitchen, oh, so many laughs and stories shared there. Garden, it remind me of Ukraine. Each space holds piece of my heart.

interview_script.question: Who do you turn to when problems arise?
interview_script.answer: Always family first. My daughter, she is wise and knows so much. We solve problems together, with her husband too. And, um, my church friends, they are like family also, always listening when I need.

interview_script.question: One tough moment in the last year?
interview_script.answer: Ah, it was when I had to go for surgery. I was scared, you know? Hospitals, they are not much fun. It was hard because, um, I worry about language, if doctor understand me. But family, they were there every step, so I not alone.

interview_script.question: How did it affect you?
interview_script.answer: It make me, um, realize importance of health, and how lucky I am to have family support. It was scary time, yes, but it also show me strength I have inside and remind me, life is precious.

interview_script.question: How did you cope?
interview_script.answer: I pray lot, kept busy with little things like knitting, to keep mind from worry too much. And, um, I talk with family daily. They give me strength, you know? Once surgery done, I focus on recovery, little goals each day like small walks.

interview_script.question: What helps when you're overwhelmed?
interview_script.answer: Taking deep breaths, sitting quietly with tea, or maybe small prayer helps. Usually I call my daughter, we talk. Talking things out makes me feel, um, lighter. And sometimes just, uh, baking bread and smelling it, that simple thing help too.

interview_script.question: What do you want life to look like in a few years?
interview_script.answer: I hope to be healthy, see grandkids grow, achieve their dreams. Maybe learn English more, be confident to hold conversation anywhere. I'd love to travel more, see more of America, maybe visit Ukraine again too.

interview_script.question: What do you want to be different?
interview_script.answer: I want to feel more independent, like with language, so I not rely on family for everything. Also, maybe have community of more older people who experience same, you know, who are learning and adjusting like me.

interview_script.question: Before Duolingo, how did you handle language learning?
interview_script.answer: Before, I listen to English radio, watch TV with subtitles, try to, um, catch some words. My daughter, she buy English books, but reading alone was hard. I try Rosetta Stone once, but it was, oh, how you say, complex? Not for babushka brain, I think. So, mostly it was slow progress.

interview_script.question: Most annoying part of old method?
interview_script.answer: It was, um, slow and not interactive. I mean, reading books, repeating lines, it gets boring, yes? Also, trying to learn without, um, feedback, you never know if you say right or wrong. It felt lonely, no connection.

interview_script.question: Time it really failed?
interview_script.answer: Oh, I remember once, I try to order in restaurant, use English from book. But, waiter, he did not understand me. I was embarrassed, but also, it was, um, wake-up call that I need better way to learn. That's when I start looking for options.

interview_script.question: How did you first hear about Duolingo?
interview_script.answer: My grandkids, they are savvy with these things. They come to me and say, 'Babushka, try Duolingo, it’s fun, like game!' and they helped me set up on phone. Such smart kids!

interview_script.question: What convinced you to try it?
interview_script.answer: When my grandkids say it's like game, and when I see how it remind me daily, I thought, 'Okay, Olga, it's time to try something new.' Also, they were excited, and I want to join their excitement, you know?

interview_script.question: Walk through a recent Duolingo use.
interview_script.answer: Ah, let's see, last time I open Duolingo, it say 'Olga, ready to learn?' I pick lesson on food, 'cause I love learning kitchen words. It start with picture of apple, then sound plays, and I repeat, 'apple.' Then it ask to match pictures with words. I got two wrong, but not worry, I learn. Later, small green owl appear, say, 'Great job!' and I feel good! Then, I earn some lingots, which, um, feel like little victory. Each lesson is like, yes, step closer to mastering English!

interview_script.question: Most helpful part?
interview_script.answer: I think, um, the structure. It keeps me on track, like little bird in forest path. Reminders, they help too, say, 'Olga, time to learn!' It very encouraging. Also, hearing pronunciation is very good, teach me how to say words right.

interview_script.question: Most frustrating part?
interview_script.answer: Sometimes, words I learn, they don't, um, seem useful. I mean, like, tricky words, not kitchen or family words, you know? And when I get it wrong, it make me feel, oh, bit silly. But, I tell myself, 'Keep trying, Olga.'

interview_script.question: Most frustrating part of Duolingo overall?
interview_script.answer: I think, maybe not enough real conversation practice. I learn, but talking with people, it’s different story. Also, app sometimes, it move too fast, like it's in hurry. I wish it slow down, let me catch breath.

interview_script.question: One time that frustration showed up?
interview_script.answer: Ah, yes. Once, I try to use word I learn in grocery store. But, um, cashier, she not understand me. I felt, like, oh, I need more practice! Words on app are one thing, but real people, they talk fast, with emotion. I need more real world practice, you know?

interview_script.question: Do you use workarounds?
interview_script.answer: Sometimes, I, uh, ask grandkids to practice with me, like small role-play. Also, I use, um, sticky notes around house with words. It help to see them daily. And, sometimes I watch English shows, repeat what they say.

interview_script.question: What do workarounds give you that Duolingo doesn't?
interview_script.answer: They give me, um, context, and, how you say, real life application. I mean, practice with family, it's more natural. Plus, I can ask questions, get instant answer, which Duolingo cannot do. It's, um, more interactive, personal.

interview_script.question: Worst-case scenario in this space?
interview_script.answer: Worst case, I guess, is, um, not understanding important conversation, like at doctor, or missing something grandkids say. It, um, makes me feel isolated, like I miss piece of life here. That's why I keep learning, don't want that happen.

interview_script.question: When you open Duolingo, what do you hope it does?
interview_script.answer: I hope it help me feel more confident in English, like each lesson build my skills. I want it to be fun, not just, um, like school. And I hope, it bring me closer to talking freely with people outside.

interview_script.question: How do you know Duolingo worked?
interview_script.answer: When I can, you know, have small talk with cashier, or understand part of conversation on TV. Also, when grandkids say, 'Wow, Babushka, you said that right!' It feels like win.

interview_script.question: One thing you'd change about Duolingo?
interview_script.answer: I would like, um, more conversation practice, you know, real scenarios. Maybe option to, uh, chat with other learners. It would be nice to hear more natural speaking, like in real life.

interview_script.question: One thing you'd change about the whole problem space?
interview_script.answer: Oh, I think, more community support, like groups of learners in same boat as me. We could meet, share struggles, practice together, maybe drink tea. It make learning less lonely, you know?

interview_script.question: Anything important we didn't cover?
interview_script.answer: I think we talk lots today. I just, um, want to say, learning is journey. Must be patient, enjoy process, even when hard. And thank you for listening to my stories!

interview_script.question: Permission to build a digital twin?
interview_script.answer: Oh, I don't know what that is, dear. But if it help someone learn, then sure, you have my blessing!
